item.title: Quantum interference keeps two atoms bound despite enough energy to break apart
item.description: How can something remain intact when it should naturally break apart? This question has been addressed by researchers at RPTU. Their work has led to the experimental observation of an unusual quantum state in which two atoms remain bound together even though they possess enough energy to separate. The results have been published in the journal Nature Physics.

item.title: Quantum gas microscope reveals individual atoms in first tunable three-component Hubbard system
item.description: For the first time, an international team of researchers from Germany, Thailand, India, China and the United States has created a three-component Hubbard system with tunable interactions in the laboratory. In doing so, the team used a quantum gas microscope to make the individual atoms visible. The study, published in Science, provides an important foundation for future quantum simulations of nuclear physics and materials science.

item.title: Atomic defects leave telltale optical fingerprints in quantum material
item.description: The tiny atomic defects so important for future quantum technologies can be difficult to spot. Fortunately, they leave behind some clues. The defects can alter how a material responds to light, producing a distinctive optical fingerprint that scientists can measure. The challenge is figuring out which fingerprints belong to which defects.

item.title: Did Life Begin in an RNA World?
item.description: Some believe the earliest life emerged from self-copying molecules that could mutate and even evolve. But that may not have been enough. The post Did Life Begin in an RNA World? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: A carefully timed pair of light pulses can amplify the motion of atomic layers in a quantum material
item.description: The principle "Work smarter, not harder!" apparently also applies to controlling quantum materials with light. Many of their fascinating properties depend on how the atoms are arranged in the crystal. Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to alter these structures in a targeted way—the light first excites electrons, whose changed energy and dynamics exert forces on the atomic nuclei and can thereby set the atoms in motion. Such processes unfold within femtoseconds, a millionth of a billionth of a

item.title: Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics
item.description: A magnet barely wider than a human hair is one of the fastest spinning objects ever and could be useful for both fundamental physics experiments and in quantum technology

item.title: A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality
item.description: Albert Einstein fought to save our everyday notion of reality from the strangeness of quantum mechanics. But those who set out to aid him keep poking holes in his argument. The post A Strange Quantum Theorem Has Killed Einstein’s Reality first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Electrical control of an unconventional quantum transport state demonstrated in a magnet for the first time
item.description: Researchers at Tohoku University and the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) have successfully controlled a unique quantum phenomenon—the quantum-geometric nonlinear Hall (QgNLH) state—using electric current for the first time. The breakthrough was achieved by revealing and exploiting the coupling between the spin structure and the QgNLH state in an electrically switchable chiral antiferromagnet.

item.title: A new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit
item.description: A recent study published in Nature Electronics and carried out by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware research group, Quantum Motion, London Center for Nanotechnology, Imperial College London and the University of Cambridge introduces a new superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit fabricated in a commercial complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) process.

item.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
item.description: By injecting “thoughts” directly into large language models, researchers are trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection. The post New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Testing Einstein's laws from the bottom of the Mediterranean Sea
item.description: Are the laws of physics truly the same everywhere in the universe? This fundamental principle, known as Lorentz invariance, lies at the heart of Einstein's theory of relativity. Yet some theories that seek to reconcile gravity with quantum physics suggest that it might not always hold. To investigate this possibility, researchers from the international KM3NeT collaboration analyzed 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events detected by KM3NeT/ORCA, a neutrino telescope located deep in the Medit

item.title: ‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds
item.description: Physics is generally built on observations, then the maths that supports them comes later. Columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan takes a look at an effort to reverse this and rebuild the laws of physics from the maths up

item.title: High-pressure setup unlocks detailed measurements of organized structures in turbulent flows
item.description: Turbulent flows are ubiquitous: they are found in clouds, in the ocean and even on other planets. Yet despite their chaotic nature, they also form large-scale structures that can be calculated and predicted. For example, while long streaks of clouds may appear orderly from the outside, their interiors are characterized by intense turbulence.

item.title: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
item.description: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property.

item.title: Is Schrödinger’s cat both dead and alive? No, it’s just haunted by its past
item.description: A radical new approach suggests some of quantum theory’s most bizarre and inexplicable effects might be down to physics failing to account properly for time

item.title: Weird ‘ultraquantum’ turbulence seen for the first time
item.description: An experiment with ultracold potassium atoms has revealed details of a type of turbulence that only exists in the quantum realm and relies on odd tangles of stringy whirlpools

item.title: 哈雷：不止于彗星
item.description: 哈雷彗星每隔76年重返地球视线。 精准预测彗星回归的哈雷，对宇宙的探索不止于此。他是一个纯粹的行动派，受好奇心驱使，用一生丈量地球。

item.title: 他们来听相对论，还是来看爱因斯坦？
item.description: 1925 年春天，阿尔伯特・爱因斯坦开启一场长途巡回讲学之旅，先前往阿根廷，之后继续到访乌拉圭与巴西。在这本旅行日记中，这位举世闻名的科学家、人道主义代表人物记下了对所见之人、所到之地的即时观感与深度思考。部分耐人寻味的段落，毫无保留地展现出他对到访东道国的真实看法。 本版完整呈现了爱因斯坦这段为期三个月旅途写下的全部日记，为人们展现了这个科学巨人更为真实复杂的一面。

item.title: 一家新型研发机构的十年：“新”在哪里？
item.description: 一个科学慈善、科技创新与全球健康交织的中国故事，以及一家新型研发机构的机制探索。

item.title: 孕期“嘴馋”，大脑里发生了什么？
item.description: 最新研究显示，怀孕会增强小鼠大脑血清素神经元内一种名为SK3的钾离子通道的活性，使参与抑制食欲的神经元变得不那么活跃，进而让孕鼠更容易出现对高热量食物的渴求。

item.title: 人类数学家的反击：N-S方程证明正确性存疑
item.description: OpenAI宣称解决纳维-斯托克斯方程（Navier-Stokes equations，简称N-S方程）问题近两个月后，数学界仍未就OpenAI是否真正解决这一问题达成共识。截至11月2日，N-S方程问题在克雷研究所官网上尚未被列为“已解决问题”。

item.title: 为什么大型犬比小型犬老得更快？
item.description: 最新研究显示，一种负责抑制“跳跃基因”活动的调控机制，随着大型犬年龄增长而减弱得更明显。这可能与大型犬衰老更快、寿命更短有关。

item.title: 香格里拉，曾经是什么模样？
item.description: 1933年，英国作家詹姆斯·希尔顿（James Hilton）在其小说《消失的地平线》（Lost Horizon）中，描述了一个名叫“香格里拉”的世外桃源。

item.title: 一位教授来信：这所高校“顶风作案”，把教师推到KPI传送带
item.description: 2026年10月9日，《中共中央 国务院关于发展新质生产力的意见》（下称“意见”）正式发布。其中第十九条写得明白而具体：“加快推动科研人员考核评价激励与报项目、发论文、评奖励等适度脱钩，防止简单按人才帽子定薪酬、定职称、定待遇。”

item.title: 延安大学的白老师，倒在“横向科研经费”指标之下？
item.description: 延安大学鲁迅艺术学院副教授白保国，据传留下了一封绝笔信，信中对学校的横向科研经费到账指标等提出强烈质疑。

item.title: 劝不动爸妈去医院的年轻人，找来了阿福
item.description: 身在杭州的阿铛放心不下。劝说无果后，她打开了常用的健康AI蚂蚁阿福。

item.title: Air holes turn silicon wafers into flat ultraviolet focusing mirrors for compact optics
item.description: Traditional lenses and mirrors focus light using curved surfaces. Metasurfaces can achieve similar functions with a flat layer of nanoscale structures that locally control the phase of light. Extending these flat optics into the ultraviolet could support compact systems for high-resolution imaging, spectroscopy, and sensing, but it introduces a fundamental materials problem: many of the materials used to make metasurfaces strongly absorb UV light.

item.title: Scientists achieve record-breaking low temperature on China's space station, paving the way for new physics experiments
item.description: Matter starts to behave differently at extremely low temperatures, creating conditions ideal for studying quantum physics and new states of matter. Now, researchers from China have achieved a new low-temperature record aboard their Tiangong space station. Their research, recently published in Science, might lead to a new generation of experiments in quantum physics and precision measurements in space.

item.title: How palm orientation shapes spin characteristics in volleyball jump serves
item.description: A new biomechanical study has uncovered how elite volleyball players control ball spin during jump serves, offering fresh scientific insight into one of the sport's most decisive offensive skills.

item.title: After 40 years of searching, physicists find evidence for an ultrarare particle decay
item.description: Physicists at CERN report that they've detected evidence of a rare meson particle decay (B⁰→ µ⁺µ⁻) that occurs when the meson's beauty quark annihilates with a down-type quark. The pair decays into a muon and antimuon, which are particles similar to electrons. Because evidence for this decay helps test theoretical predictions from the Standard Model, physicists have been waiting for it since 1984, when it was first theorized.
